---
title: "Quiz: attention, transformers and pretrained models"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** In one sentence each: how does a $3 \times 3$ convolution combine pixels, and how does self-attention combine tokens?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where do the weights come from?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A convolution takes a weighted sum of the 9 neighbours with fixed learned weights that depend only on the relative position and are the same everywhere. Self-attention takes a weighted average of all tokens, with weights computed from the content (how well each token's key matches the query) and normalised to sum to 1.
:::

---

**Q2.** Scores $2, 0, 0$ for three values $6, 3, 0$. Compute the attention output.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Softmax: $e^2, e^0, e^0$ normalised.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Weights $e^2/(e^2 + 2) = 0.787$, and $0.106$ twice. Output $0.787 \cdot 6 + 0.106 \cdot 3 + 0 = 5.04$.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why does a transformer without position codes not know where a patch is in the image?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Shuffle the patches.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Attention treats the tokens as a set: shuffling the input only shuffles the output in the same way (permutation equivariance). Nothing in the computation depends on the order, so the arrangement of the patches is invisible unless a position code is added to each token.
:::

---

**Q4.** Halving the patch size of a transformer multiplies the number of attention weights per layer by how much?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Number of tokens, then its square.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Four times as many tokens, so $4^2 = 16$ times as many weights.
:::

---

**Q5.** You have 15 annotated images and a large pretrained network. Frozen features + a linear probe, or full fine-tuning? Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many parameters are trained in each case?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Frozen features + a probe: only a few dozen parameters are trained, which 15 images can determine; full fine-tuning of millions of weights on 15 images overfits and can destroy the useful pretrained features.
:::

---

**Q6.** A contrastive model was pretrained with strong brightness augmentation. Why is it a poor feature extractor for measuring the intensity of a stain?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What were the two views taught to agree on?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It was trained so that a crop and its brightened copy have the same embedding: brightness is exactly what it learned to ignore. The augmentations decide what the features are blind to.
:::

---

**Q7.** A network says 0.99 for 1000 test images and is right on 920. Is it calibrated? What does temperature scaling with $T > 1$ do to its accuracy?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare confidence and accuracy.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No: confidence 0.99, accuracy 0.92: overconfident. Temperature scaling lowers the confidences but leaves the predicted classes, and so the accuracy (92 %), unchanged.
:::

---

**Q8.** Temperature was fitted on validation data from microscope A. Will the network be calibrated on microscope B?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What changed between A and B?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not necessarily: under domain shift the accuracy drops while the confidences need not, so the network is typically overconfident again. Calibration must be checked (and refitted) on data from B.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Why is the dot product in attention divided by $\sqrt d$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Variance of a sum of $d$ independent products.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For queries and keys with independent unit-variance entries, $\mathbf q^\top\mathbf k$ has variance $d$. Without scaling the scores grow with $d$ and the softmax saturates (one token gets all the weight, gradients vanish); dividing by $\sqrt d$ brings the variance back to 1.
:::

---

**Q10.** Give two situations in which a classical method is the better choice than a deep network.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Data, prior knowledge, explanation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For example: very few images or no annotations; a strong prior on the shape (circles, lines, a calibration grid) that a model fit uses directly; a measurement whose bias must be understood and explained; or when a simple classical pipeline already works on all the data.
:::
